title: Where do you seek me?
hookLine: in a Kabir song, God names the holy places of two faiths and says: I'm in neither
tomorrow: what's swinging between two poles in Kabir's song, and who's on it?

cards: People cross oceans to stand in one holy place. Theo has the opposite problem. His sister is marrying in the church he grew up in and left, and he isn't sure he can walk back through those doors.

So here's an odd detail for him. In one of Kabir's songs, God is the speaker, and God names the holy places of two faiths: the Kaaba in Mecca, where Muslims turn to pray, and Mount Kailash, Shiva's mountain.
And God says: I'm in neither. Why would a poet who loved God turn down the best addresses on earth?

teach.h: O SERVANT, WHERE DOST THOU SEEK ME?
teach.b: Hear how it opens, in Tagore's English: "O servant, where dost thou seek Me? Lo! I am beside thee. I am neither in temple nor in mosque: I am neither in Kaaba nor in Kailash."
Then it turns down rites, ceremonies, even yoga and renunciation. It isn't sneering at pilgrims. It picks the very best places on purpose.

teach.h: NOT KEPT THERE, SO NOT KEPT OUT.
teach.b: If God isn't kept even there, God isn't kept anywhere, and so God isn't kept out of anywhere either.
The song ends: "Kabîr says, 'O Sadhu! God is the breath of all breath.'" Kabir has a little story for the same idea, in a couplet.

teach.h: THE MUSK DEER HUNTS ITS OWN SCENT.
teach.b: A musk deer smells the sweet scent of musk and runs through the whole forest hunting for it. It never finds it. The musk is in its own body.
That's the teaching under the puzzle, and it's Kabir's center: God isn't far off at a holy address; God is as near as breathing, and is met by remembering, not by traveling.

teach.h: SUMIRAN: THE NAME, AS NEAR AS BREATH.
teach.b: The poets of his line called that remembering sumiran, keeping the name close with each breath.
So for Theo, the song cuts both ways. In Kabir's song, that church isn't the only place God lives. And it isn't a place God has left, either.

how: Kabir's 'where do you seek me' song is sung as a bhajan, often from its Hindi opening, 'moko kahan dhoondhe re bande'; in the sant tradition, remembering God's name with the breath (sumiran) is a daily practice.

games.q: what does “where do you seek me?” mean?
o: a teacher's riddle about which temple is holiest
Kabir's question, asked in God's voice, to a searcher
a pilgrim's question when he's lost on the road

games.q: the song and its pieces: tap the pairs.
p: hunts a scent that's in its own body
remembering the name with the breath

s: Kabir's song says temples and mosques are worthless
it says God isn't kept in them. its point is how near God is, not that buildings are bad.
in this song, God is the one speaking
'O servant, where dost thou seek Me? Lo! I am beside thee.'
in Kabir's couplet, the deer finds the musk deep in the forest
it never finds it. the musk was in its own body all along.

games.q: a coworker saves all year for a pilgrimage and asks if Kabir would call it pointless. what fits the song?
o: yes: Kabir says the trip is a waste of money
no: the trip is fine, but God isn't kept at the end of it
no: Kabir says God lives most at the holy places
games.why: the song isn't against travel; it's against thinking God is far. God is beside the traveler the whole way.

practice: Rest one hand on whatever is nearest: a chair arm, a blanket, the floor. Let it stay there, and feel your breath come and go underneath it. Nothing to travel to; just what's beside you, and the breath.

wordCard.voice: Where do you seek me?: Kabir's question, asked in God's own voice, to the one who's searching far away.

orig.note: Hindi, the song's opening as it's sung: where do you search for me, O servant?

carryVoice: Hold on to this: beside you, not kept in any building and not kept out of one. Two of eight with Kabir.
